title: Position: Every Ground Truth is a Human Construction, not an Objective Truth
claim: Outcomes that look like a single objective reference are shaped by a chain of human choices, and different choices yield different references.
layout: Single panel, top-to-bottom, colored horizontal bands with crossing colored paths ending in outputs
description: A single vertical diagram titled 'Ground truth construction pathways'. Five horizontal colored bands, from top to bottom, are labeled: 'Where / when / whom to observe' (red), 'How (what features) to observe' (orange), 'Who defines the label ontology' (yellow), 'Who labels the observations' (green), and '[And so on]' (gray). Gray circular nodes sit in three columns inside each band. Three colored arrows (blue, red, purple) enter at the top and weave through different nodes, crossing each other. Each arrow switches columns between bands, showing different choices at each stage. Dotted arrows leave the last band and point to GT1, GT2 and GT3. Under the labels are three versions of the same landscape photo: vivid color, sepia, and a black-and-white binary mask. The eye goes first to the crossing colored paths.
caption: Every ground truth is { constructed} as the result of multiple decisions, not a single objective truth. Different pathways yield different ground truths (GT1, GT2, GT3, ...) for the same task.
abstract: Ground truth datasets play a fundamental role as reference values in the training and evaluation of machine learning models. This position paper argues that ground truths are not neutral objective measurements that are naturally given, but instead that they are constructed by arrangements of humans and technologies. We argue that the ML community will benefit from articulating and discussing these often invisible or unreported choices and acknowledging that reference data sets are contingent, not universal. Focusing on the situated and context-dependent nature of ground truths can improve reliability by enabling a better informed perspective on where, when, and how the datasets, and the models they have shaped, can best be used. We argue for increasing `situated reliability' which includes articulating the limits and strengths of models and their truth claims. Finally, paying more attention to the construction of ground truths can support transparency, accountability, and interdisciplinary work.
